In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the carcinogenic action of DMN is potentiated by partial hepatectomized, but not by intact, rats; that DEN is a more potent carcinogen for intact rats than for partially hepatectimized ones; and that MMS is not carcinogenic in either group.
the carcinogenic action of DMN, but not DEN or MMS, was potentiated by partial hepatectomized animals, and that this potentiation occurred only during the wave of cellular DNA replication.

the alkylating agents, DMN and DEN, are capable of inducing liver carcinomas in rats, when administered after partial hepatic resection, and that the carcinogenic effect is not dependent on the presence of regenerating tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a single treatment with DMN or DEN, but not with MMS, can induce liver cell cancer in rats after a single injection, when administered during the period of rapid DNA replication after partial hepatectoromy.
the initiation of carcinogenesis can occur at the time of the first DNA replication following a carcinogen exposure.
DMN and DEN are carcinogens in the liver, but only when the DNA of the liver cells is being replicated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a single treatment of a carcinogen is a useful tool for studying the initiation of cancer.

we have shown for the first time that a single treatment with a chemical carcinogen can initiate liver carcinomas in rats, and that the incidence of liver carcinomas is highest if the carcinogen is administered during the wave or DNA synthesis which follows partial hepactectomy.
the use of the alkylating agent, methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) as a model for studying the mechanism of initiation is not justified.
